body:
What geographical information systems do

A Geographical Information System (GIS) is used to store, manage, analyse and display information linked to locations. In disaster management, GIS helps answer questions such as which settlements overlap a flood zone, which roads pass through potentially affected terrain and where exposed public facilities are concentrated.

GIS does not itself predict every disaster or establish how much damage will occur. Its main advantage is that information from different sources can be examined together using a common geographical reference.

Three types of information that must be distinguished

InformationWhat it representsExample
HazardLocation, extent, intensity or probability of a dangerous eventArea that may be inundated in a specified flood scenario
ExposurePeople and assets in the potentially affected areaSchools and households lying within that flood extent
Vulnerability and capacitySusceptibility and ability to manage consequencesHousing conditions and access to safe routes

A hazard map represents the physical threat. An exposure map identifies the people or assets that may encounter that threat. A risk map seeks to communicate possible consequences by bringing hazard information together with exposure, vulnerability and, where appropriate, capacity. The exact meaning of the term risk map depends on the method used and must be checked in the map's legend and documentation.

How layers are combined

A GIS may contain a base map of settlements and roads, a terrain-elevation layer, a mapped flood extent and locations of schools or health centres. These layers can be superimposed, or overlaid, to identify geographical intersections.

Suppose a flood-inundation layer covers part of a village and overlaps the location of a school. The immediate conclusion is that the school is exposed under that scenario. The overlay alone does not prove that the building will collapse, that its occupants will be present when flooding occurs or that it will suffer a specified monetary loss. Such conclusions require additional information.

Typical steps in an assessment

  1. Define the question: Identify the hazard, geographical area and planning purpose.
  2. Prepare hazard information: Use relevant historical records, observations or modelled hazard extents.
  3. Locate exposed assets: Add population, settlement and infrastructure information.
  4. Consider vulnerability and capacity: Assess conditions affecting the severity of consequences.
  5. Interpret and verify: Identify priority areas and examine the results against local knowledge.

Role of remote sensing and ground information

Remote sensing obtains information about the Earth's surface without direct physical contact, commonly through satellites or aircraft. Satellite imagery can help identify land cover, settlement expansion and the geographical extent of some floods. Ground observations, such as field surveys or river gauges, can provide local information that imagery alone may miss.

GIS, remote sensing and satellite navigation are related but distinct. GIS is the system used for geographical analysis. Remote sensing supplies observations. Satellite navigation systems help determine locations. Combining them can improve mapping, but none eliminates uncertainty.

Reading a risk map correctly

Every map should be interpreted using its legend, scale, hazard scenario, source date and data resolution. A coloured region may represent hazard intensity, exposure, vulnerability or estimated risk, depending on the map. A colour has no universal meaning across all disaster maps.

Small-scale or low-resolution maps may be suitable for identifying broad regional patterns but unsuitable for deciding whether a particular house will be flooded. In addition, a map of long-term flood susceptibility is different from a map of flooding observed during a current event.

Spatial overlap is a screening result, not proof of damage. The quality of a GIS-based assessment depends on the accuracy, completeness and update frequency of its hazard and exposure layers.

Prelims focus

  • GIS combines information associated with geographical locations.
  • A hazard map shows the physical threat; an exposure map shows potentially affected people or assets.
  • A risk assessment requires more than locating people inside a hazard zone.
  • Remote sensing supplies observations; GIS supports analysis of geographically referenced data.
  • Map interpretation depends on the legend, scale, scenario and data quality.
  • Trap: An asset inside a mapped flood zone is exposed, not necessarily damaged.

[UN-SPIDER Knowledge Portal, 'Recommended Practice: Exposure Mapping', sections 'Requirements', 'Workflow' and 'Strengths and Limitations', consulted 2 November 2026; UNDRR, 'Risk and Resilience Metrics: Methodology', section 'Geographic distribution of hotspots for key hazards across the country', including interpretation and limitations, consulted 2 November 2026; UNDRR, Sendai Framework Terminology, entry 'Disaster risk information', 2017, consulted 2 November 2026.]

body:
Why a risk assessment considers several possible events

The consequences of a hazard depend on its characteristics and the conditions in the affected area. A single event description is therefore often insufficient for planning. Risk assessors use scenarios to examine how different plausible events might affect the same community.

A risk scenario describes a specified possible hazardous event, the conditions under which it is assessed and the consequences that may follow. It supports planning; it is not necessarily a forecast that the event will occur.

For a river settlement, one scenario might consider a frequently occurring moderate flood. Another might examine a less frequent but more extensive flood. A third might consider flooding during a period when an important access road is already unusable. These scenarios help reveal different needs and weaknesses.

Historical, plausible and severe-event scenarios

Scenarios can be informed by recorded events, scientific modelling and knowledge of local conditions. A historical scenario examines an event similar to one already observed. A plausible future scenario examines conditions that could reasonably occur. A severe-event scenario helps identify possible consequences when hazardous conditions are particularly serious.

The severity of a scenario does not itself tell us its probability. A severe scenario may be useful for preparedness even when it is less likely than a moderate one. Equally, a frequent moderate event can create substantial cumulative losses if exposed communities experience repeated disruption.

Multiple, compound and cascading hazards

Hazards should not always be considered in isolation. A cyclone may bring strong winds, intense rain and coastal storm surge. Rainfall can contribute to flooding, while damaged electricity or communication facilities may make it harder to receive information and maintain essential services.

When hazardous conditions occur together or their effects interact, the resulting situation may be more serious than an assessment of only one hazard suggests. A cascading impact occurs when an initial event or disruption contributes to further disruptions.

For example, a coastal community may face storm surge and heavy rainfall during the same cyclone. If roads become waterlogged, access to a shelter or health facility may be more difficult. The assessment must consider the location of the community, the condition of access routes and its capacity to act on warnings. The existence of a cyclone warning does not mean every linked consequence will occur.

Where uncertainty enters the assessment

Uncertainty means that the available information or method does not establish an outcome with complete precision. It may arise from several sources:

  • Natural variability: The exact location, timing or intensity of future hazardous events may be unknown.
  • Incomplete observations: Rain gauges, field surveys or past event records may not capture every relevant condition.
  • Model assumptions: Different assumptions about rainfall, terrain or the physical event can produce different hazard extents.
  • Exposure-data limitations: Population and building records may be outdated or geographically coarse.
  • Vulnerability assessment: Selected indicators and their relative importance may not fully represent local conditions.

An uncertain estimate is not necessarily useless. It can still identify important exposure patterns and help compare possible actions, provided the uncertainty is made clear. For instance, a broad district map may reliably suggest that a floodplain deserves closer study while remaining too imprecise for an individual property's assessment.

How scenarios support preparedness

Authorities may use scenarios to identify settlements needing better warning coverage, check whether essential routes remain accessible, decide where public information is most needed and review arrangements for protecting vulnerable groups. Comparing several scenarios is generally more informative than treating one estimated outcome as certain.

Risk assessments should be reviewed when new hazard evidence becomes available or when population, land use, infrastructure or local capacities change. This is particularly important where reliance on historical records alone may not represent changing future conditions.

Prelims focus

  • A scenario is a specified possible event and its assessed consequences, not necessarily a forecast.
  • Likelihood and severity are different characteristics of a scenario.
  • A cyclone may produce wind, heavy rainfall and storm surge in the same event.
  • Cascading impacts arise when one disruption contributes to further disruptions.
  • Uncertainty can arise from observations, model assumptions, exposure records and vulnerability indicators.
  • Trap: A detailed scenario is not a guarantee that the described event will happen.

[UNDRR, Sendai Framework Terminology, entries 'Disaster risk assessment' and 'Disaster risk', 2017, consulted 2 November 2026; UNDRR, 'Risk and Resilience Metrics: Methodology', sections on probabilistic modelling and spatial-data limitations, consulted 2 November 2026; NCERT, India: Physical Environment, Class 11 Geography, chapter 6, 'Natural Hazards and Disasters', reprint 2025–26, sections on cyclones and floods; WMO, 'Early Warnings for All', section on multi-hazard early warning systems, consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Risk Scenarios, Multiple Hazards and Uncertainty

body:
From knowing the risk to protecting people

Risk assessment identifies places and communities that may suffer harm. An early warning system uses risk knowledge, hazard observations, forecasts, communication arrangements and preparedness measures to help people take protective action before or during a hazardous event.

An early warning system is not merely a forecasting instrument or an alert sent to a phone. It must connect scientific information with the people who need it and the actions they can realistically take. A technically accurate forecast provides limited protection if exposed communities never receive the message or do not understand what it requires.

A people-centred, end-to-end early warning system links knowledge of disaster risk, monitoring and forecasting, communication of warnings, and preparedness for appropriate action.

The 4 essential pillars

1. Disaster risk knowledge

Communities and authorities need information about the hazards they face, the people and assets exposed, the factors that increase vulnerability and the capacities already available. Hazard and risk maps help identify where an alert is most important and who may require additional assistance.

2. Detection, observation, monitoring, analysis and forecasting

Relevant agencies collect observations and analyse changing conditions. Rainfall, river levels, weather patterns and sea-level observations are examples of information that may be used for different hazards. Where scientific forecasting is possible, models and expert interpretation help estimate how an event may develop.

3. Warning dissemination and communication

Warnings must reach the people and institutions at risk. Messages should identify the threat, affected area, expected time and necessary precautions. They should be communicated through channels accessible to the intended audience and in languages people understand.

4. Preparedness and response capabilities

People must know what to do when a warning arrives. Preparedness includes public awareness, agreed local arrangements, accessible safe places where applicable and regular review of communication and response plans. Communities need practical capacity to act, not just information about a possible hazard.

How risk mapping and early warning fit together

Consider a river settlement identified through flood-risk mapping. The map shows which low-lying neighbourhoods may be affected. Monitoring and forecasting identify developing rainfall and river conditions. The responsible services issue a warning when warranted. Local communication systems then help residents receive information and follow the appropriate public guidance.

The risk map and the warning perform different functions. The map supplies information about where potential harm may be concentrated. The warning communicates an emerging or expected hazard and the need for action within a specified period.

Multi-hazard early warning systems

A multi-hazard early warning system addresses more than one hazard and seeks to account for situations in which hazards occur together, in sequence or with interacting effects. For example, weather information, flood information and coastal warnings may all matter during a severe cyclone affecting a river-mouth settlement.

However, the existence of a multi-hazard system does not mean that every hazard can be predicted with equal accuracy or lead time. Earthquake occurrence cannot presently be predicted by specifying its exact date, location and magnitude. Tsunami-warning systems instead use observations after a potentially tsunamigenic event to assess and communicate coastal danger.

Early Warnings for All

The international Early Warnings for All initiative seeks to expand protection through effective early warning systems by the end of 2027. Its framework identifies the 4 pillars described above. The target is an international programme objective, not evidence that universal protection has already been achieved.

Prelims focus

  • Risk knowledge is Pillar 1 of the Early Warnings for All framework.
  • Detection, observation, monitoring, analysis and forecasting form Pillar 2.
  • Warning dissemination and communication form Pillar 3.
  • Preparedness and response capabilities form Pillar 4.
  • The international Early Warnings for All initiative has an end-of-2027 protection objective.
  • Trap: Issuing a technically correct forecast alone does not complete an effective early warning system.

[World Meteorological Organization, 'Overview of the Early Warnings for All: Executive Action Plan 2023–2027', WMO Bulletin, 5 May 2023, section on the 4 pillars; WMO, 'Early Warnings for All', programme overview, consulted 2 November 2026; UNDRR, Sendai Framework Terminology, 'Disaster risk assessment', 2017, consulted 2 November 2026; U.S. Geological Survey, 'Can You Predict Earthquakes?', consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Early Warning Systems and Their Four Essential Pillars
